lesson.title: No Shortcuts: Why the Mean Value Theorem's Hypotheses Matter
lesson.summary: Both of the Mean Value Theorem's requirements, continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval, are load bearing. Drop either one and you can build a function where no point matching the average rate of change exists at all.
lesson.body:
It is tempting to treat continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) as boilerplate that most reasonable looking functions satisfy anyway. But both conditions are doing real work, and the cleanest way to see that is to build functions that violate exactly one condition and watch the guaranteed point c fail to exist.

For a differentiability failure, take f(x) = |x| on the interval [-1, 1]. This function is continuous everywhere, including on the closed interval [-1,1], so that half of the hypothesis is fine. But it is not differentiable at x = 0, which lies in the interior of the interval, because the graph has a sharp corner there: the slope is -1 approaching from the left and +1 approaching from the right, and no single tangent line exists at that corner. The average rate of change over [-1,1] is [f(1) - f(-1)] / [1 - (-1)] = (1 - 1)/2 = 0. If the Mean Value Theorem applied, there would be some c in (-1,1) with f'(c) = 0. But f'(x) equals -1 for every x less than 0 and +1 for every x greater than 0, and it is undefined exactly at the one point, x = 0, where it might have been 0. No point in (-1,1) has f'(c) = 0. The guarantee genuinely fails, and the single missing derivative at one interior point is entirely responsible.

For a continuity failure, define g(x) = x^2 for 0 is less than or equal to x, and x is less than 1, and separately set g(1) = 0. This function agrees with x^2 everywhere except that its value has been artificially reset at the right endpoint, creating a jump discontinuity there: as x approaches 1 from the left, x^2 approaches 1, but g(1) is defined to be 0, so g is not continuous on the closed interval [0,1]. It is, however, differentiable on the open interval (0,1), since it matches the smooth function x^2 everywhere strictly between 0 and 1. The average rate of change is [g(1) - g(0)]/(1-0) = (0-0)/1 = 0. If the theorem applied, some c in (0,1) would satisfy g'(c) = 0. But g'(x) = 2x on (0,1), which equals 0 only at x = 0, and x = 0 is an endpoint, excluded from the open interval (0,1). So again, no c exists in the open interval, and the single discontinuity at the boundary point x = 1 is what breaks the guarantee.

Both examples share the same structure: pick a candidate average rate, 0 in both cases, and then show that no instantaneous rate anywhere in the open interval actually reaches it. That is exactly what the Mean Value Theorem rules out when its hypotheses genuinely hold, which is why checking continuity on the full closed interval and differentiability on the open interval is never a box to check absentmindedly; it is the reason the conclusion is trustworthy at all.
